title: Graphic Design Fundamentals for Creators and Marketers
subtitle: Design scroll-stopping posts, ads and thumbnails with hierarchy, layout, type, colour and clean exports
description:
You do not need a design degree to make work that looks professional — you need a small set of principles applied consistently. This course teaches the fundamentals that working designers use every day: visual hierarchy, alignment and spacing, grids and composition, typography, colour theory and accessible contrast, and choosing and treating imagery.

Everything is applied to the formats creators and small teams actually ship: social posts, carousels, stories, ads and video thumbnails. You will learn how to work with templates without looking templated, how tools such as Canva and Figma organise frames, components and styles, and how to export files that stay sharp after platforms compress them. Each lesson ends with a practical exercise, and the final assessment uses realistic scenarios so your certificate reflects skills you can use on the job.
outcomes: Build a clear visual hierarchy so viewers read a design in the order you intend
Lay out posts, ads and thumbnails on a grid with consistent margins, alignment and spacing
Choose, pair and size typefaces for legibility on small mobile screens
Create colour palettes and check text contrast against WCAG accessibility ratios
Select, license and treat images so they support the message instead of competing with it
Use templates, components and styles in design tools without producing generic work
Export files in the right format, size and colour space for each platform

lessons.title: Visual hierarchy: controlling what people see first
lessons.body:
### Why hierarchy is the whole game

People do not read designs; they scan them. On a social feed a viewer decides in a fraction of a second whether your post is worth a second look. Visual hierarchy is the deliberate ordering of elements so the eye lands on the most important thing first, the second most important thing next, and so on. If everything shouts, nothing is heard.

A useful mental model is the **three-level hierarchy**:

1. **Primary** — the one thing the viewer must get even if they look for one second (a headline, a face, a product, a number).
2. **Secondary** — the supporting context that makes the primary make sense (a subheading, a short benefit, a date).
3. **Tertiary** — details for people who are already interested (handle, logo, URL, fine print).

Most weak designs fail because they have two or three competing primaries.

### The levers that create hierarchy

You control attention with a small set of levers. Each one works by creating *difference*.

| Lever | How it creates emphasis | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Size | Bigger elements are seen first | Headline, hero product |
| Weight | Bold text pulls ahead of regular | Key phrase inside a sentence |
| Colour and value | High contrast or a saturated accent draws the eye | Call to action, price |
| Position | Top-left (in left-to-right languages) and centre get early attention | Headline placement |
| Isolation | An element surrounded by space stands out | A single statistic or quote |
| Faces and eyes | Humans look at faces, then where the eyes point | Thumbnails, ads |
| Motion | Movement beats stillness | Animated stickers, video |

Note the reading-direction point: for Arabic or Urdu audiences, designs read right-to-left, so the natural entry point and the flow of the layout mirror. If you design bilingual posts for audiences in Pakistan, the UAE or Saudi Arabia, plan the layout for each script instead of flipping a finished design.

### The squint test

The fastest hierarchy check is to blur your vision. Step back from the screen, squint (or apply a heavy blur to a screenshot) and ask: what is the first blob I see, and what is second? If the answer is not your primary and secondary message, adjust the levers.

A related check is the **one-second test**: show the design to someone for about one second, hide it, and ask what it was about. If they cannot tell you, your primary element is not dominant enough.

### Worked example: a webinar announcement

A creator posts an announcement with this content: "Free live workshop", "Grow on short-form video in 30 days", date and time, the host's photo, the host's handle and a "Save your seat" button.

**First draft problems:** the words "Free live workshop" are in the largest type, the benefit is small, the date is the same size as the benefit, and the photo is a tiny circle in the corner. The eye bounces between four things.

**Redesign using the three levels:**

- Primary: the benefit headline, "Grow on short-form video in 30 days", set large and bold.
- Secondary: the host's photo, large enough to read the face, plus "Free live workshop · Thu 7 pm" in a medium size.
- Tertiary: handle and a small "Save your seat — link in bio" line.

The accent colour is used only on the call to action, so it does not compete with the headline. The squint test now shows one dominant block of text and a face — exactly the intended order.

### A hierarchy checklist you can reuse

```
[ ] I can state the single primary message in one sentence
[ ] The primary element is clearly the largest or highest-contrast item
[ ] There are no more than 2–3 distinct text sizes
[ ] Accent colour is reserved for one or two elements
[ ] Tertiary details are small, grouped and out of the way
[ ] The design passes the squint test and the one-second test
```

### Common mistakes

- **Making everything bold.** Emphasis only works relative to non-emphasised elements.
- **Too many sizes.** Five slightly different font sizes read as noise; use clear steps.
- **Logo as primary.** Unless the post is about the brand itself, the logo is usually tertiary.
- **Decorative elements stealing focus.** Arrows, stickers and shapes should point to the message, not become it.
- **Ignoring the context.** Your post sits in a feed next to other bright posts; hierarchy must work at thumbnail size, not only full screen.

### Summary

Hierarchy is decided before you touch a tool: write down your primary, secondary and tertiary content, then use size, weight, colour, position and space to make that order visible. Test it by squinting and by showing it to someone for a second.

video.script: Every design you publish is competing for about one second of attention. In that second, the viewer's eye needs somewhere obvious to land. That is what visual hierarchy does: it decides what people see first, second and third. Start before you open any tool. Write down your primary message — the one thing someone must understand even if they barely look. Then your secondary message, the context that makes the first one make sense. Everything else is tertiary: your handle, your logo, the fine print. Now use the levers of attention to make that order visible. Size is the strongest: the biggest element usually wins. Weight and contrast come next — bold, dark or brightly coloured elements pull ahead. Position matters, because readers of left-to-right languages tend to start at the top left, while Arabic and Urdu readers start at the top right. Isolation matters too: one element surrounded by empty space feels important. And never underestimate faces. People look at faces first, then follow where the eyes are pointing. The most common mistake is emphasising everything. If the headline, the price, the logo and the button are all big and bold, nothing stands out and the viewer scrolls on. Here is a quick test. Step back from your screen and squint until the design blurs. What is the first shape you notice? What is second? If that is not your primary and secondary message, adjust size, contrast or spacing until it is. Then try the one-second test: show someone the design briefly, hide it, and ask what it was about. Hierarchy is not decoration. It is the order of your message, made visible.

keyTakeaways: Hierarchy is the deliberate order in which viewers notice elements — decide it before designing.
Use a three-level structure: primary, secondary and tertiary content.
Size, weight, colour, position, isolation and faces are the main levers of attention.
The squint test and one-second test reveal whether your intended order actually works.

knowledgeCheck.question: A post has a headline, a price, a logo and a call to action all in the same large bold type. What is the core problem?
options: The logo should be larger than everything else
There is no clear primary element, so nothing stands out
The colours are probably wrong
The design needs more decorative elements
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Emphasis is relative: when four items share the same size and weight, none is dominant and the eye has no entry point. Colour and decoration do not fix a missing hierarchy, and enlarging the logo usually makes it worse.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does the squint test help you check?
options: Whether text is spelled correctly
Whether the image resolution is high enough
Whether the colours meet brand guidelines
Which elements dominate when detail is removed
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Blurring removes detail so only size, contrast and mass remain — which reveals the real visual order. It says nothing about spelling, resolution or brand compliance.

knowledgeCheck.question: You are adapting an English post for an Arabic-speaking audience. What is the best approach to hierarchy?
options: Mirror the finished English layout exactly with a flip tool
Plan the layout for right-to-left reading so the entry point and flow suit the script
Remove all text and rely only on images
Keep the English layout because hierarchy is universal
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Right-to-left reading changes the natural entry point and flow, so the layout should be planned for that script. Blindly flipping can mirror photos, logos and numbers incorrectly, and ignoring direction weakens the hierarchy.

lessons.activity: Take one of your recent posts and write its primary, secondary and tertiary content on paper. Redesign it so the squint test shows that order, then compare before and after side by side.

lessons.title: Contrast, repetition, alignment and proximity
lessons.body:
### Four principles that fix most layouts

Designer and educator Robin Williams popularised four principles, often remembered as **C.R.A.P.**: contrast, repetition, alignment and proximity. They are not the only principles in design, but together they explain why most amateur layouts feel messy and how to fix them quickly.

### 1. Contrast — make different things *very* different

Contrast is how you signal that two elements have different roles. The key word is *very*. A heading at 22 px next to body text at 18 px looks like a mistake; a heading at 40 px next to 18 px body text looks intentional.

Ways to create contrast:

- Size (large versus small)
- Weight (bold versus light)
- Colour and value (dark versus light, saturated versus muted)
- Typeface (a display face for headings, a plain sans-serif for body)
- Shape and texture (a rounded button against a rectangular layout)

**Rule of thumb:** if two elements are not meant to be the same, do not make them *almost* the same.

### 2. Repetition — make the design feel like one system

Repetition means reusing the same choices consistently: the same heading style, the same accent colour, the same corner radius, the same icon style, the same spacing. Repetition creates unity inside a single post and recognisability across a series. It is why a creator's carousels are recognisable before you read the handle.

Practical repetition choices for a content series:

```
Heading font + size:     e.g. Bold sans, 64 px
Body font + size:        e.g. Regular sans, 28 px
Accent colour:           one colour, used only for highlights
Corner radius:           same on every card and button
Margin:                  same on every slide (e.g. 80 px)
Slide number / progress: same position on every slide
```

### 3. Alignment — nothing placed arbitrarily

Every element should be visually connected to something else on the page through a shared edge or centre line. Alignment creates invisible lines that make a layout feel organised.

- **Left alignment** is the most readable for multi-line text in left-to-right languages, because each line starts at the same point. (Right alignment plays that role for Arabic and Urdu.)
- **Centre alignment** works for short, symmetrical content such as a quote or a single headline, but long centred paragraphs are harder to read because every line starts in a different place.
- **Mixing alignments** on one design (a centred headline, left-aligned body, right-aligned logo) usually looks accidental unless there is a clear grid.

Use your tool's alignment and distribute functions rather than nudging by eye. Turn on smart guides or snapping.

### 4. Proximity — group related items

Items that belong together should sit close together; unrelated items should be further apart. Proximity lets viewers understand structure without lines or boxes.

A classic error: equal spacing between everything. If the gap between a heading and its paragraph is the same as the gap between that paragraph and the next heading, the viewer cannot tell which heading owns which text. The fix is simple — tighten the space inside a group and increase the space between groups.

### Whitespace: the principle behind the principles

Whitespace (or negative space) is any empty area, whatever its colour. It is not wasted space. It separates groups, frames the primary element and makes a design feel confident and premium. Crowded designs feel cheap and are harder to read on small screens.

### Worked example: fixing a promotional flyer

**Before:** a sale flyer with five fonts, text centred and left-aligned at random, the discount the same size as the terms and conditions, and every item spaced evenly.

**After applying the four principles:**

1. *Contrast:* the discount becomes the dominant element — very large, heavy weight, accent colour. Terms shrink to small, light text.
2. *Repetition:* two typefaces only; the accent colour reused on the call to action; consistent corner radius on the product cards.
3. *Alignment:* everything left-aligned to one margin, product cards on a three-column grid.
4. *Proximity:* each product image sits tight with its name and price; bigger gaps separate the cards and the footer.

### Quick audit table

| Principle | Question to ask | Common fix |
|---|---|---|
| Contrast | Are different roles clearly different? | Increase size or weight steps |
| Repetition | Are styles reused consistently? | Create text and colour styles |
| Alignment | Does every element share an edge or axis? | Align to one margin or grid |
| Proximity | Are related items grouped? | Tighten inside groups, widen between |

### Common mistakes

- Using contrast timidly (small size differences).
- Adding a new style for every element instead of reusing styles.
- Centring everything by default.
- Filling every empty area with icons, stickers or patterns.

### Summary

When a design feels "off" but you cannot say why, run the four-principle audit. It will usually point to weak contrast, inconsistent styles, loose alignment or confusing spacing.
keyTakeaways: Make different elements clearly different — timid contrast looks like a mistake.
Repeat styles, colours and spacing to create unity and a recognisable series.
Align every element to a shared edge or axis; avoid random centre/left mixes.
Group related items with proximity and separate groups with more space.
Whitespace is an active design tool, not wasted space.

knowledgeCheck.question: A carousel's heading is 24 px and its body text is 22 px. Which principle is being applied too weakly?
options: Proximity
Alignment
Repetition
Contrast
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The size difference is too small to signal a different role, so it reads as an error. Contrast needs to be decisive; the other principles concern grouping, consistency and shared edges.

knowledgeCheck.question: Viewers cannot tell which subheading belongs to which paragraph because all gaps are equal. What is the best fix?
options: Put every paragraph in a coloured box
Use a different font for each section
Tighten the gap between each subheading and its paragraph and increase the gap between groups
Centre all the text
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Proximity communicates grouping: small gaps inside a group, larger gaps between groups. Boxes can help but add clutter, while centring and extra fonts do not solve the grouping problem.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is left alignment usually preferred for multi-line body text in English?
options: It uses less space
It automatically increases contrast
Each line starts at the same point, which makes reading easier
Platforms require it
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A consistent starting edge helps the eye find the next line. It is not a platform rule, does not save space, and has nothing to do with contrast.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which choice best supports repetition across a 10-slide carousel?
options: Using a different photo filter per slide
Using a new accent colour on every slide for variety
Changing the layout completely on each slide
Keeping heading style, margins and slide-number position identical on every slide
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Repetition means consistent styles and positions, which creates unity and recognisability. Constant variation in colour, layout or filters breaks the system.

lessons.activity: Audit one flyer, post or slide you have made using the four-question audit table. Make one fix for each principle and note which change made the biggest difference.

lessons.title: Gestalt, eye flow and guiding the viewer
lessons.body:
### How the brain groups what it sees

Gestalt psychology describes how people perceive visual elements as organised wholes rather than separate parts. You do not need the theory in depth, but a handful of Gestalt principles explain why some layouts feel instantly clear.

| Principle | What people perceive | Design application |
|---|---|---|
| Proximity | Close items belong together | Group image, title and price in a product card |
| Similarity | Items that look alike are related | Same colour for all clickable elements |
| Closure | The mind completes incomplete shapes | Logos and icons that use implied lines |
| Continuity | The eye follows lines and curves | Arrange items along a path toward the call to action |
| Figure–ground | We separate a subject from its background | Keep subjects distinct from busy backgrounds |
| Common region | Items inside a boundary are grouped | Cards, panels and background blocks |

The practical lesson: you can create structure with space, similarity and regions instead of adding lines, borders and labels everywhere.

### Figure–ground in real life

Figure–ground problems are the most common cause of illegible social graphics. White text over a bright sky, a product photographed against a similar-coloured backdrop, or a logo on a busy pattern all make it hard to separate subject from background.

Fixes, from least to most intrusive:

1. **Reposition** the text over a calmer area of the image.
2. **Darken or lighten** the whole image slightly (an overlay at low opacity).
3. **Add a gradient** from transparent to dark behind the text only.
4. **Use a solid block** or card behind the text.
5. **Blur or simplify** the background, or choose a different image.

### Eye-flow patterns

Research on reading behaviour, including eye-tracking studies by usability researchers, describes common scanning patterns. Treat these as tendencies, not laws:

- **Z-pattern:** on simple, image-led designs with little text, the eye tends to move from top-left across to the top-right, diagonally down, then across the bottom. Useful for ads and single-message posts: headline top, visual in the middle, call to action bottom-right.
- **F-pattern:** on text-heavy screens, people read the first lines more fully and then scan down the left side. Useful for carousels and infographics: front-load key words at the start of lines and headings.
- **Focal-point flow:** a strong visual element (a face, a bright object) captures attention first; the viewer then moves to nearby elements. Useful for thumbnails.

For right-to-left languages these patterns mirror.

### Directional cues

You can actively steer the eye:

- **Gaze:** if a person in the image looks toward your headline, viewers tend to follow the gaze. If they look out of the frame, attention leaks away.
- **Lines and shapes:** roads, arms, arrows and leading lines in photos guide the eye along a path.
- **Pointing and gestures:** a hand pointing at a product works because it is a natural cue.
- **Sequence numbering:** in carousels and infographics, numbered steps tell people the order explicitly.

### Worked example: a product ad

A skincare brand has a photo of a model holding a bottle, a headline "Hydration that lasts all day", and a "Shop now" button.

- **Version A:** the model looks straight at the camera; the headline is at the bottom-left; the button is top-right. The eye goes to the face, then wanders.
- **Version B:** the model looks toward the bottle, which sits near the headline; the headline is top-left; the button sits bottom-right where a Z-pattern ends. The eye goes face → bottle → headline → button.

Version B is not guaranteed to perform better — only testing can show that — but it is structurally clearer, which gives it a better chance.

### An eye-flow planning template

```
Entry point (what is seen first):   ______________
Path (what the eye moves to next):  ______________ → ______________
Exit / action (where it ends):      ______________
Cues used (gaze, lines, numbers):   ______________
Distractions to remove:             ______________
```

### Common mistakes

- **Gaze leading out of the frame** toward nothing.
- **Call to action placed where the eye never goes**, such as a tiny corner above the headline.
- **Too many focal points**: three faces, two products and a bright sticker all competing.
- **Assuming a pattern is universal**: always consider reading direction and test with real viewers.

### Summary

Use Gestalt principles to create structure without clutter, fix figure–ground problems before publishing, and plan a deliberate path from entry point to action using gaze, lines and sequence.
keyTakeaways: Gestalt principles (proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, figure–ground, common region) create structure without extra decoration.
Poor figure–ground separation is a leading cause of illegible text on images.
Z- and F-patterns are useful tendencies, mirrored for right-to-left languages, not fixed laws.
Gaze, lines, gestures and numbering can deliberately steer the viewer toward your call to action.

knowledgeCheck.question: White headline text sits over a bright cloudy sky and is hard to read. What is the least intrusive first fix to try?
options: Make the text smaller
Add a thick drop shadow and outline to every letter
Move the text to a calmer, darker area of the image
Replace the photo with a stock illustration
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Repositioning solves the figure–ground problem without altering the image. Heavy effects look dated, shrinking text makes legibility worse, and replacing the image is a last resort.

knowledgeCheck.question: Making every clickable element the same colour applies which Gestalt principle?
options: Continuity
Similarity
Figure–ground
Closure
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Similarity means elements that look alike are perceived as related — so consistent colour signals 'these are all actions'. Closure, continuity and figure–ground describe other perceptual effects.

knowledgeCheck.question: In a thumbnail, the person pictured is looking out of the right edge of the frame, away from the title. What is the likely effect?
options: Viewers' attention tends to follow the gaze out of the frame, away from the title
It automatically increases click-through rate
It improves text contrast
It has no effect on attention
knowledgeCheck.explanation: People tend to follow gaze direction, so looking away from the title pulls attention away from it. It has no automatic performance benefit and is unrelated to contrast.

lessons.activity: Pick a design you like from a brand you admire. Sketch its eye path using the planning template, noting entry point, cues and action. Then apply the same path to one of your own designs.

lessons.title: Grids, margins and a spacing system
lessons.body:
### Why grids make you faster, not more rigid

A grid is a set of invisible guides — columns, rows, margins and gutters — that tells you where things can go. Professionals use grids not because they lack creativity but because a grid removes hundreds of small decisions. Once the structure is fixed, you can focus on content.

### Anatomy of a grid

| Part | What it is | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Margins | Space between content and the canvas edge | Keeps content away from edges and platform UI |
| Columns | Vertical divisions of the live area | Gives consistent widths for text and images |
| Gutters | Gaps between columns | Prevents content from touching |
| Rows / baseline | Horizontal divisions or a text rhythm | Aligns elements vertically |
| Live area | The area inside the margins | Where important content should sit |

### Choosing a grid for social formats

For most social and ad work, simple is best:

- **Single-column with generous margins** — quotes, announcements, single statistics.
- **Two-column** — before/after, comparisons, image plus text.
- **Three- or four-column** — product grids, feature lists, infographics.
- **Modular grid** (columns plus rows) — dense carousels or information graphics.

A popular approach for a 1080 px wide canvas is a margin in the range of roughly 60–100 px with a 4- or 6-column grid inside it. The exact numbers matter less than using the same ones every time.

### A spacing system

Random gaps (13 px here, 22 px there) create subtle messiness. A **spacing scale** fixes that by limiting you to a few values. Many digital design teams use multiples of 4 or 8.

```
Spacing scale (8-point based)
xs   8
sm   16
md   24
lg   40
xl   64
xxl  96

Use:  inside a group → sm/md
      between groups → lg/xl
      canvas margin  → xl/xxl
```

This directly supports proximity: small values inside groups, large values between groups.

### Safe zones and platform UI

Social platforms overlay interface elements on your design: profile names, captions, buttons, progress bars and — for vertical video — like, comment and share icons down one side. Content in those areas can be hidden.

Good practice:

- Keep headlines, faces, logos and calls to action inside a **central safe area**, well away from the top and bottom edges of 9:16 designs and away from the side where action buttons appear.
- Check the platform's current guidance or preview tool before publishing — overlays change as apps are redesigned.
- In ads, platforms often provide safe-zone templates; use them.

### Setting up a reusable grid (tool-neutral steps)

1. Create a canvas at the target size (for example 1080 × 1350 px for a 4:5 portrait post).
2. Add margin guides on all sides.
3. Add a column grid inside the margins (for example 6 columns with 24 px gutters).
4. Add horizontal guides for the safe area if designing vertical formats.
5. Save the file as a template or a frame you duplicate for every new post.

In Figma this is a layout grid applied to a frame; in Canva you can show rulers and guides and add custom guides. Other tools have equivalents.

### Worked example: a three-tip carousel slide

Canvas 1080 × 1350 px, 80 px margins, 6-column grid, 24 px gutters.

- Slide number in the top-left of the live area.
- Headline spans all 6 columns, starting at the top margin plus 64 px.
- Supporting text spans 5 columns, leaving one empty column on the right for breathing room.
- A small icon sits in column 1 beside each tip; text starts at column 2.
- Handle sits bottom-left inside the margin on every slide.

The result looks consistent across slides without extra effort, because every slide shares the same structure.

### Breaking the grid on purpose

Once the grid is established, you can break it deliberately — a photo that bleeds off the edge, a huge number that overlaps a column. Breaking a grid only reads as intentional when everything else respects it.

### Common mistakes

- **No margins**: text touching the edge looks cramped and may be cropped.
- **Inconsistent margins between slides**, which makes swiping feel jumpy.
- **Ignoring platform overlays**, hiding the call to action behind buttons.
- **Too many columns** for simple content, leading to fussy layouts.

### Summary

Set margins, columns and a spacing scale once, respect safe zones, and save it as a template. Consistency across posts will come almost automatically.
keyTakeaways: A grid's margins, columns and gutters remove small decisions and create consistency.
Use a limited spacing scale (for example multiples of 8) instead of arbitrary gaps.
Keep critical content inside platform safe zones and verify current overlays before publishing.
Break the grid only deliberately and only when everything else respects it.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the main purpose of a spacing scale such as 8, 16, 24, 40, 64?
options: To increase file resolution
To limit spacing to consistent values so layouts feel orderly
To define brand colours
To meet platform upload requirements
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A spacing scale standardises gaps, supporting proximity and consistency. It has nothing to do with resolution, upload rules or colour.

knowledgeCheck.question: A creator's call-to-action text on a 9:16 story keeps getting hidden. What is the most likely cause?
options: The text sits in an area covered by platform interface elements
The file format is wrong
The font is a serif
The colour palette is too small
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Vertical formats have overlays such as reply bars and buttons near the edges; content there can be obscured. Format, font style and palette would not hide the text.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which grid would usually suit a simple quote graphic best?
options: A different grid for each word
A single column with generous margins
No margins at all
A 12-column modular grid
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Simple content needs a simple structure; a single column with generous margins frames the quote. Complex grids add fussiness and no margins look cramped.

lessons.activity: Build a reusable 4:5 template with margins, a column grid and a written spacing scale. Recreate one of your existing posts inside it and compare the consistency.

lessons.title: Composition, balance and focal points
lessons.body:
### Composition is arrangement with intent

Composition is how elements are arranged inside the frame to create a focal point, a sense of balance and a path for the eye. It applies equally to photos you shoot, images you crop and layouts you build.

### Balance: symmetrical and asymmetrical

- **Symmetrical balance** mirrors elements around a central axis. It feels stable, formal and calm — useful for announcements, luxury products and quotes.
- **Asymmetrical balance** distributes different elements so their *visual weight* balances. A large light area can balance a small dark area. It feels dynamic and modern — useful for ads, thumbnails and editorial posts.

**Visual weight** increases with size, darkness, saturation, texture, and faces or text (people are drawn to both). Elements further from the centre also feel heavier, like a lever.

### Classic compositional tools

| Tool | What it is | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| Rule of thirds | Divide the frame into a 3×3 grid; place key subjects on the lines or intersections | Portraits, product shots, thumbnails |
| Centred composition | Subject in the middle, often symmetrical | Bold single-subject posts, logos, quotes |
| Leading lines | Lines in the image lead toward the subject | Lifestyle and travel photos |
| Framing | Surround the subject with a natural frame (doorway, hands) | Adds depth and focus |
| Negative space | Large empty area around a small subject | Premium, minimal, space for text |
| Scale contrast | One very large element against small ones | Drama and emphasis |

The rule of thirds is a helpful starting point, not a law. Centred compositions are very effective on mobile, where the frame is small and bold.

### Cropping as composition

Much design work involves cropping existing photos. Good cropping:

- Removes distractions at the edges.
- Gives the subject room to "look into" the frame.
- Avoids cutting people at joints (wrists, knees, ankles) and avoids slicing through the top of the head in an awkward place — cropping into the forehead can be fine for close-ups if intentional.
- Leaves clean space where text will go.

**Tip:** when choosing photos for a series, pick images that have natural empty space on one side. They give you room for headlines without covering the subject.

### Depth and layering

Flat designs can feel lifeless. You can add depth by:

- Overlapping elements (a product slightly overlapping a text block).
- Using a cut-out subject in front of text (the "text behind subject" effect — use it sparingly and keep the text legible).
- Scaling elements to imply near and far.
- Soft shadows that are consistent in direction.

### Worked example: a thumbnail composition

A tutorial video about budgeting apps. Elements: the creator's face showing surprise, a phone showing an app, and the text "I tried 5 budget apps".

1. Canvas 16:9. Divide into thirds.
2. Creator's face on the left-third intersection, large, eyes toward the phone.
3. Phone on the right third, slightly overlapping the face for depth.
4. Text in the upper right, short — perhaps "5 APPS TESTED" — because long text is unreadable at small sizes.
5. Background simplified and slightly darkened so the face and phone pop.
6. Check at small size: reduce the canvas to phone-thumbnail scale and confirm the face, phone and text still read.

### A composition checklist

```
[ ] One clear focal point
[ ] Balance is intentional (symmetrical or asymmetrical)
[ ] Subject has room to look/move into the frame
[ ] Edges are clean — no distracting fragments
[ ] Text has a calm area to sit on
[ ] Works at small (thumbnail) size
```

### Common mistakes

- **Everything centred and the same size**, making designs static and forgettable.
- **Subject crammed against an edge** with empty space behind it.
- **Overused effects** — heavy shadows, glows and outlines layered together.
- **Composing only at full size** and never checking at thumbnail scale.

### Summary

Decide on your focal point, choose symmetrical or asymmetrical balance deliberately, use cropping and simple tools such as the rule of thirds, and always check the composition at the size people will actually see it.
keyTakeaways: Balance can be symmetrical (stable, formal) or asymmetrical (dynamic) — choose deliberately.
Visual weight grows with size, darkness, saturation, texture, faces and text.
The rule of thirds is a starting point; centred compositions are strong on mobile.
Crop to remove distractions, give subjects room and leave space for text.
Always check composition at the size viewers will actually see.

knowledgeCheck.question: A small, dark, saturated object on the right is balanced by a large, pale area on the left. What kind of balance is this?
options: No balance
Radial balance
Symmetrical balance
Asymmetrical balance
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Different elements balancing through visual weight is asymmetrical balance. Symmetrical balance mirrors elements; radial balance radiates from a centre.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which crop is usually the weakest choice for a portrait?
options: Cropping exactly at the subject's wrists and knees
Cropping so the subject looks into the frame
Cropping to remove a distracting object at the edge
Cropping to leave calm space for a headline
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Cutting at joints tends to look awkward. The other options are all good cropping practice.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why should you shrink a thumbnail design to a small size before publishing?
options: Because most viewers first see it small, so the focal point and text must still read
To test colour accuracy
To reduce file size
Because platforms reject large files
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Thumbnails are mostly seen at small sizes in feeds and search results; a composition that only works large will fail. The check is about legibility, not file size or colour.

lessons.activity: Take three photos you might use in posts. Crop each twice — once centred and once using the rule of thirds with room for text — and decide which composition supports a headline best.

lessons.title: Designing across aspect ratios and formats
lessons.body:
### One idea, many shapes

A single campaign often needs a square post, a portrait feed post, a vertical story or short-video cover, a landscape thumbnail and perhaps a banner. Designing each from scratch wastes time; stretching one design to fit every shape produces distorted or cropped results. The professional approach is to **design a system that adapts**.

### Common aspect ratios

| Ratio | Orientation | Typical use (verify current specs) |
|---|---|---|
| 1:1 | Square | Feed posts, profile images, some ads |
| 4:5 | Portrait | Feed posts and ads that take more screen space |
| 3:4 | Portrait | Some platforms' feed and grid displays |
| 9:16 | Vertical full-screen | Stories, Reels, Shorts, TikTok, vertical ads |
| 16:9 | Landscape | Video thumbnails, YouTube, presentations |
| 1.91:1 | Wide landscape | Link previews, some banners and ads |

Common pixel sizes include 1080 × 1080 (1:1), 1080 × 1350 (4:5), 1080 × 1920 (9:16) and 1280 × 720 or larger (16:9). Platforms change recommended sizes, grid crops and overlays regularly, so always check the current help pages or ad specs before a major campaign.

### Aspect ratio versus resolution

- **Aspect ratio** is the shape (width to height).
- **Resolution** is the number of pixels.

1080 × 1350 and 2160 × 2700 are the same 4:5 shape; the second has four times as many pixels. Designing at a higher resolution can help with sharp text after compression, but upload limits and file sizes still apply.

### The "core and flex" method

1. **Define the core** — the elements that must appear in every version: headline, key visual, logo or handle, call to action.
2. **Define the flex** — elements that can be dropped or moved when space is tight: secondary text, decorative shapes, extra images.
3. **Design the most demanding format first.** Often that is the 9:16 vertical (tall, with overlays) or a small thumbnail.
4. **Adapt outward.** Rearrange rather than rescale: a stacked layout in 9:16 may become side-by-side in 16:9.
5. **Keep type sizes relative to the shorter side** so text stays legible across formats.

### Adapting layouts: patterns

- **Stack ↔ side-by-side:** image above text in vertical formats; image beside text in landscape formats.
- **Crop the photo, not the subject:** choose images with space around the subject so you can crop to different ratios.
- **Re-flow text:** break headlines into more lines in narrow formats, fewer in wide formats.
- **Scale the logo proportionally** and keep it in a consistent corner.

Tool support: many design tools offer resize or "magic resize" features, and Figma supports auto layout and constraints that make frames adapt. These save time but always need a human check — automated resizing often crops faces or places text under platform overlays.

### Worked example: a product launch

Core: product photo, "New: Travel Blender", "Pre-order now", logo.

- **9:16 story:** product photo in the upper half, headline in large type below it, call to action above the bottom safe zone, logo top-left inside the safe area.
- **4:5 feed post:** product photo occupying the right 60%, headline and call to action stacked on the left 40%.
- **16:9 banner:** product on the right third, headline centred-left, logo top-left, call to action bottom-left.
- **1:1 ad:** simplified — product and headline only; call to action handled by the platform's button.

All four share fonts, colours, photo treatment and logo placement, so they look like one campaign.

### Format planning template

```
Campaign:            __________________
Core elements:       headline | visual | CTA | logo
Flex elements:       __________________
Formats needed:      [ ] 1:1  [ ] 4:5  [ ] 9:16  [ ] 16:9  [ ] other ____
Hardest format:      __________________ (design first)
Safe-zone check:     [ ] done per format
Final small-size check: [ ] done
```

### Common mistakes

- Stretching or squashing images to fill a new ratio.
- Letting automated resize tools publish without review.
- Using the same absolute type size in every format so text becomes tiny in large canvases.
- Forgetting overlays on vertical formats.

### Summary

Separate core from flex content, design the hardest format first, rearrange rather than rescale, and verify every version at real size with platform overlays in mind.
keyTakeaways: Aspect ratio is shape; resolution is pixel count — they are different decisions.
Define core elements that appear in every format and flex elements you can drop.
Design the most constrained format first, then adapt by rearranging, not stretching.
Automated resize tools save time but always need a human check for crops and overlays.

knowledgeCheck.question: 1080 × 1350 and 2160 × 2700 images share the same what?
options: Resolution
Colour profile
File size
Aspect ratio
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Both are 4:5 shapes; the second has four times the pixels, so resolution and file size differ. Colour profile is unrelated.

knowledgeCheck.question: In the core-and-flex method, what should you do with 'flex' elements in a small format?
options: Shrink them until they fit, however small
Enlarge them to fill the space
Drop or move them when space is tight
Replace them with the logo
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Flex elements are optional and can be removed or relocated so core elements stay legible. Shrinking everything makes text unreadable.

knowledgeCheck.question: After using an automatic resize feature, what is the most important next step?
options: Convert all files to GIF
Change the brand colours for each size
Publish immediately to save time
Review each version for cropped subjects, legibility and elements under platform overlays
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Automated resizing often crops faces or places text under overlays, so each version needs a human check. File format and colour changes are not the issue.

lessons.activity: Choose one message and produce it in 9:16, 4:5 and 16:9 using the core-and-flex template. Design the 9:16 version first and note what you rearranged for the other two.

modules.title: Typography that reads on every screen
modules.summary: Understand type anatomy and classification, pair typefaces, build a type scale, and keep text legible on small mobile screens.

lessons.title: Type anatomy, classification and choosing typefaces
lessons.body:
### Why type choices matter so much

Most social graphics, ads and thumbnails are mostly text. The typeface you choose sets the tone before anyone reads a word: a heavy geometric sans feels bold and modern, a high-contrast serif feels editorial or luxurious, a rounded sans feels friendly. Choosing well is less about taste and more about matching purpose, legibility and brand.

### Essential vocabulary

| Term | Meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Typeface | The design (e.g. a sans-serif family) | What you choose |
| Font | A specific style/weight file of that typeface | What you install/use |
| Family | All weights and styles of a typeface | More weights = more flexibility |
| Baseline | Line letters sit on | Alignment of mixed sizes |
| x-height | Height of lowercase letters like "x" | Larger x-height = more legible when small |
| Ascender / descender | Parts above x-height / below baseline | Affect line spacing needs |
| Serif | Small strokes at the ends of letters | Style and tone |
| Stroke contrast | Difference between thick and thin strokes | High contrast can break up at small sizes |
| Counter | Enclosed space inside letters (o, e, a) | Open counters improve legibility |

### Main classifications

- **Serif** (old-style, transitional, modern/didone, slab): tradition, authority, editorial tone. Slab serifs are sturdy and good for bold headlines. High-contrast didone faces look elegant but thin strokes can vanish at small sizes or after compression.
- **Sans-serif** (grotesque, neo-grotesque, humanist, geometric): clean and versatile; the default for screens and social. Humanist sans faces are often very legible; geometric faces feel modern.
- **Display**: decorative faces designed for large sizes only — posters, headlines, thumbnails.
- **Script / handwritten**: personality and warmth, but low legibility in long text or all caps.
- **Monospace**: every character the same width; signals code or technical content.

### Choosing a typeface: four questions

1. **Purpose:** is this for headlines, body text or both? Display faces are for headlines only.
2. **Legibility:** at the smallest size it will be seen, are letters distinct? Check pairs like I/l/1 and O/0, and look for a generous x-height and open counters.
3. **Tone:** does the personality fit the message and brand?
4. **Coverage and licence:** does it support the languages and characters you need (for example accented Latin, Arabic or Urdu scripts), and does its licence allow your use (social, ads, logo, commercial products)?

On licensing: many high-quality typefaces are available under open licences (for example the SIL Open Font License used by many families in Google Fonts). Fonts bundled in design tools have their own terms. Commercial fonts require a licence, and licences may differ for desktop, web, app and logo use. Always read the licence before using a font for a client's logo or a product for sale.

### Multi-script projects

If you design for audiences across Pakistan, the Gulf and English-speaking markets, you may need Latin and Arabic-script typefaces that work together. Look for families designed with multi-script support, or choose pairs whose weight and proportions feel compatible. Urdu is often typeset in the Nastaliq style, which needs more vertical space and specific font support; test with real text, not placeholder text.

### Worked example: choosing type for a fitness coach

Brand personality: energetic, direct, trustworthy. Formats: Reels covers, carousels, story ads.

- Headline: a bold, condensed or geometric sans in heavy weight — punchy and space-efficient for short phrases.
- Body: a humanist sans in regular and semi-bold — highly legible for tips and captions on slides.
- Rejected: a thin script (illegible on small screens) and a didone serif (feels like fashion, not fitness, and thin strokes suffer on mobile).

### A typeface selection checklist

```
[ ] Tested at the smallest real size (on a phone, not only on desktop)
[ ] Distinct I / l / 1 and O / 0
[ ] Enough weights (at least regular + bold)
[ ] Supports all required languages and characters
[ ] Licence covers intended use (social, ads, logo, merchandise)
[ ] Tone matches brand personality
```

### Common mistakes

- Using a display or script face for body text.
- Choosing fonts on a large desktop monitor and never checking on a phone.
- Using a font from a free download site without checking the licence.
- Faking bold or italic with software effects instead of using the real weights.

### Summary

Learn the vocabulary, pick from the right classification for the job, test legibility at real size, and check language coverage and licensing before committing.
keyTakeaways: A typeface is the design; a font is a specific weight/style of it.
Large x-height, open counters and distinct characters improve legibility at small sizes.
Display and script faces are for headlines and accents, not body text.
Always check language coverage and the licence for your intended use.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which feature most improves legibility of text at small sizes?
options: Very tight letter spacing
Very high stroke contrast
A relatively large x-height and open counters
Decorative swashes
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A generous x-height and open counters keep letters distinct when small. High contrast, swashes and tight spacing reduce legibility.

knowledgeCheck.question: A client wants to use a font downloaded from a free font site in their new logo. What should you do first?
options: Rename the font file
Check the font's licence to confirm logo and commercial use are allowed
Use it — free fonts can be used anywhere
Convert it to outlines so the licence no longer applies
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Licences vary and may restrict commercial or logo use. Converting to outlines or renaming does not remove licence obligations.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which is the best use of a display typeface?
options: Long paragraphs of body copy
Form labels on a website
Large headlines and short phrases
Legal terms and fine print
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Display faces are designed for large sizes and short text. Body copy, fine print and labels need highly legible text faces.

lessons.activity: Shortlist three typefaces for your brand or a client. Test each on a phone at the smallest size you would use, check the characters I, l, 1, O and 0, and confirm the licence terms.

lessons.title: Type pairing, scale and spacing
lessons.body:
### How many typefaces do you need?

For most creators and small brands, **one or two typeface families** are enough. A single versatile family with several weights can carry an entire brand. Two families — one for headlines, one for body — add personality. Three or more usually creates visual noise unless managed by an experienced designer.

### Pairing principles

Good pairs have **contrast with harmony**: different enough to create hierarchy, similar enough to feel related.

| Pairing approach | Example structure | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Superfamily | Sans and serif versions of the same family | Very safe, cohesive |
| Serif headline + sans body | Editorial serif + neutral sans | Classic, trustworthy |
| Sans headline + sans body (weights) | Heavy sans + regular sans of the same family | Modern, clean |
| Display headline + neutral body | Distinctive display + humanist sans | Personality with legibility |

Avoid pairing two faces that are *almost* the same (two similar geometric sans-serifs), which looks like an error, and avoid pairing two faces that both demand attention (two decorative display faces).

### Building a type scale

A type scale is a defined set of sizes you reuse. Designers often use a ratio (for example 1.25 or 1.333) to generate harmonious steps. For social canvases around 1080 px wide, a practical scale might be:

```
Display   96 px   (one big number or word)
H1        64 px   (headline)
H2        44 px   (subheading)
Body      32 px   (main text on slides)
Small     24 px   (labels, handle, footnotes)
```

Treat these as starting points; check them on a phone. Text on social graphics usually needs to be much larger than you would guess from designing on a desktop.

### Spacing: leading, tracking and kerning

- **Leading (line height):** space between lines. Body text often reads well around 1.3–1.5 times the font size. Large headlines usually need tighter leading (around 1.0–1.2) or they look loose.
- **Tracking (letter spacing):** uniform spacing across a word or line. All-caps text often benefits from slightly increased tracking; large headlines can sometimes take slightly tighter tracking.
- **Kerning:** adjusting space between specific letter pairs (such as "AV" or "To"). Most good fonts are well-kerned; manually check large headlines and logos.

### Line length and alignment

Very long lines tire the eye and very short lines break reading rhythm. For body text on websites, a common guideline is roughly 45–75 characters per line. On social slides, lines are much shorter, so keep sentences concise and break lines at natural phrase boundaries rather than mid-phrase.

Avoid **widows and orphans** (a single word left alone on the last line) in headlines — adjust line breaks manually.

### Emphasis without chaos

Choose one method of emphasis per level:

- Bold for key phrases in body text.
- Colour highlight for one or two words in a headline.
- Avoid combining underline, italic, bold, colour and all caps on the same phrase.

**All caps:** effective for short labels and punchy headlines, but slower to read in long passages because word shapes become uniform rectangles.

### Worked example: fixing a tips carousel

**Before:** four fonts; headline 40 px, body 36 px (weak contrast); body leading 1.0 (cramped); long centred paragraphs; random bold, italic and underline.

**After:**

1. One family: bold weight for headings, regular for body.
2. Scale: H1 64 px, body 32 px, small 24 px.
3. Body leading 1.4, headline leading 1.1.
4. Left-aligned body text, max about 8–10 words per line.
5. One emphasis rule: accent colour on one keyword per headline.

### Type style sheet template

```
Heading font:  ________  weight ___  size ___  leading ___  tracking ___
Subhead font:  ________  weight ___  size ___  leading ___
Body font:     ________  weight ___  size ___  leading ___
Small text:    ________  weight ___  size ___
Emphasis rule: ______________________
Alignment:     ______________________
```

Save these as text styles in your design tool so every new design uses them automatically.

### Common mistakes

- Too many typefaces or weights.
- Sizes that are almost the same.
- Default leading on large headlines, making them look loose.
- Stacking multiple emphasis styles.

### Summary

Use one or two families, define a type scale with clear steps, set leading and tracking intentionally, and save everything as reusable text styles.
keyTakeaways: One or two typeface families are enough for most brands.
Pair faces with contrast and harmony; avoid near-identical or competing pairs.
A defined type scale with clear steps creates consistent hierarchy.
Body text needs looser leading than large headlines; use one emphasis method per level.

knowledgeCheck.question: Two very similar geometric sans-serif typefaces are paired for headline and body. What is the likely result?
options: Better accessibility
It looks like an accidental inconsistency
Automatically better brand recognition
Strong, clear hierarchy
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Near-identical faces lack contrast, so the difference reads as a mistake. Good pairs are clearly different yet harmonious.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which leading is typically most appropriate for multi-line body text?
options: 3 times the font size
Leading does not matter for body text
0.8 times the font size
Around 1.3–1.5 times the font size
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Body text reads comfortably with moderate leading around 1.3–1.5. Very tight leading makes lines collide; very loose leading breaks the text into separate lines.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is long text in all caps harder to read?
options: All caps cannot be kerned
Word shapes become uniform, removing cues the eye uses to recognise words
All-caps fonts are always low resolution
Platforms penalise all-caps text
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Mixed case creates distinctive word shapes; all caps flattens them into rectangles. Resolution, platform penalties and kerning are not the reason.

lessons.activity: Write a type style sheet for your brand using the template, create matching text styles in your design tool, and apply them to one existing carousel.

lessons.title: Legibility on mobile, video and thumbnails
lessons.body:
### Designing for the thumb-scroll

Most social content is viewed on a phone, often briefly, sometimes in bright sunlight, and sometimes by people with low vision. Legibility — how easily individual letters and words can be read — is non-negotiable. If people cannot read it at a glance, the rest of your design work is wasted.

### The minimum-size mindset

There is no single universal minimum size for social graphics, because canvases are scaled down to different screen widths. Instead, use tests:

1. **Phone preview test:** send the design to your phone and view it at the size it appears in the feed, not zoomed in.
2. **Arm's-length test:** hold the phone at a normal distance. Can you read every piece of text you intend people to read?
3. **Thumbnail test:** for video thumbnails and carousel covers, view at the small size they appear in search results or grids.

If a piece of text fails, make it larger, shorten it, or remove it. Fine print that must be present for legal reasons (for example ad disclosures or terms) still needs to be readable.

### Word count discipline

- **Thumbnails:** aim for very few words — often three to five — because they compete with the video title that already appears next to them. The thumbnail text should complement the title, not repeat it.
- **Story and short-video text:** keep each on-screen phrase short enough to read in the time it is visible.
- **Carousel slides:** one idea per slide; use more slides rather than cramming.
- **Ads:** the headline should communicate the offer alone; details can live in the caption or landing page.

### Text on images and video

Techniques to keep text readable over imagery:

| Technique | When to use | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| Solid text block or card | Busy or colourful backgrounds | Can feel heavy if overused |
| Gradient scrim | Photos with a darker or calmer area | Keep it subtle |
| Overall darken/lighten | Evenly busy images | Can dull the photo |
| Outline or stroke | Bold, playful thumbnail styles | Thin outlines look cheap; keep weight consistent |
| Subtle shadow | Slight separation | Heavy shadows look dated |

For video captions and subtitles: use a clean sans-serif, sufficient size, high contrast (for example white text with a dark backing or outline), and position within safe zones so platform UI does not cover them. Burned-in captions help viewers who watch without sound and improve accessibility, but also keep platform-generated or uploaded caption files where available so captions can be read by assistive tech and adjusted by users.

### Accessibility considerations for text

- Maintain strong contrast between text and background (covered in detail in the colour module).
- Do not rely on very thin weights for important text.
- Avoid placing text over moving or flashing backgrounds.
- Include important information in the caption or alt text as well, because screen readers cannot read text baked into an image. Many platforms let you add alt text to images — use it.

### Worked example: a YouTube-style thumbnail

Video title: "How I Edit Videos 3× Faster With Keyboard Shortcuts".

- **Weak thumbnail:** full title repeated in small text across the top, a screenshot of the editing software, tiny keyboard icon.
- **Strong thumbnail:** large, bold text "3× FASTER" (two words), a close-up of hands on a keyboard or the creator's expressive face, a high-contrast background, and the text positioned away from where the platform shows the video duration badge (commonly the bottom-right corner).

The text adds curiosity and complements the title rather than duplicating it.

### Legibility QA checklist

```
[ ] Viewed on a phone at real feed/thumbnail size
[ ] Every intended piece of text readable at arm's length
[ ] No important text in thin or script weights
[ ] Text-to-background contrast checked
[ ] Word count minimal for the format
[ ] Text clear of platform overlays (duration badge, buttons, captions)
[ ] Key information also in caption / alt text
```

### Common mistakes

- Designing on a large monitor and trusting how it looks there.
- Repeating the video title in the thumbnail.
- Using thin, elegant fonts for important words on busy photos.
- Forgetting alt text and captions, excluding screen-reader users and people watching on mute.

### Summary

Test on a real phone at real size, keep word counts ruthless, separate text from imagery with scrims or blocks, and support accessibility with captions and alt text.
keyTakeaways: Test legibility on a real phone at feed and thumbnail size, not zoomed in on a monitor.
Use very few words on thumbnails and complement the title rather than repeating it.
Separate text from busy imagery with blocks, scrims or careful positioning.
Burned-in captions and alt text make content accessible and usable on mute.

knowledgeCheck.question: What should thumbnail text usually do in relation to the video title?
options: Contain the full description
Repeat the title word for word
Be omitted entirely in all cases
Complement it with a few high-impact words
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The title already appears next to the thumbnail, so thumbnail text works best as a short complementary hook. Repeating the title wastes space; long text is illegible.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why add alt text to an image that already has text baked into it?
options: It is required to upload images
It changes the thumbnail
Screen readers cannot read text inside an image, so alt text makes the content accessible
It improves image resolution
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Text inside a picture is invisible to assistive technology; alt text provides an equivalent. It does not affect resolution or uploads.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which is the most reliable way to check a design's legibility before publishing?
options: Check the file size
Zoom to 200% on a desktop monitor
Print it on A4 paper
View it on a phone at the actual size it appears in the feed
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Real-device, real-size viewing reflects how audiences see it. Zooming in or printing exaggerates legibility; file size is irrelevant.

lessons.activity: Pick your last three thumbnails or covers and run the legibility QA checklist on each. Redesign the weakest one with fewer, larger words and compare them side by side at thumbnail size.

modules.title: Colour theory and accessible contrast
modules.summary: Build purposeful palettes, use colour to create hierarchy and mood, and make sure text and graphics meet accessible contrast standards.

lessons.title: Colour theory essentials
lessons.body:
### The language of colour

Colour is one of the fastest ways to create mood, hierarchy and brand recognition — and one of the easiest ways to make a design look amateur. A little theory goes a long way.

**Three properties describe every colour:**

| Property | Meaning | Design use |
|---|---|---|
| Hue | The colour family (red, blue, green…) | Identity and mood |
| Saturation (chroma) | Intensity or purity | Vivid for accents, muted for backgrounds |
| Value (lightness) | How light or dark | Contrast, hierarchy and legibility |

Value matters most for legibility. Two colours with very different hues can have nearly identical lightness — and text in one on the other will be hard to read. Converting a design to greyscale is a quick way to check value contrast.

### Colour models you will meet

- **RGB** — red, green, blue light; used for screens. Hex codes (for example #1A73E8) are RGB written compactly.
- **HSL/HSB** — hue, saturation, lightness/brightness; intuitive for adjusting colours.
- **CMYK** — cyan, magenta, yellow, black inks; used in print. Some vivid screen colours cannot be reproduced in CMYK.
- **sRGB** — the standard colour space for the web and most social platforms. Export in sRGB unless a platform says otherwise.

### Colour harmonies

Colour-wheel relationships give reliable starting points:

- **Monochromatic:** tints and shades of one hue. Calm, elegant, easy.
- **Analogous:** neighbouring hues (blue, blue-green, green). Harmonious and natural.
- **Complementary:** opposite hues (blue and orange). High energy; great for making one element pop.
- **Split-complementary:** one hue plus the two neighbours of its complement. Vibrant but less tense.
- **Triadic:** three evenly spaced hues. Playful; needs one dominant colour.

### The 60-30-10 guideline

A practical distribution for many layouts:

- **About 60%** dominant colour — usually a neutral or background.
- **About 30%** secondary colour — panels, imagery, supporting shapes.
- **About 10%** accent — calls to action, highlights, key numbers.

It is a guideline, not a formula, but it prevents the most common mistake: using every colour equally.

### Building a small palette

For a creator or small brand, a practical palette is:

```
Primary / brand colour:   1 (recognisable, used often)
Accent colour:            1 (for actions and highlights)
Neutrals:                 3–5 (near-black, greys, off-white)
Support colours:          0–2 (optional, for charts or categories)
Functional colours:       success / warning / error (for UI work)
```

Define each colour as a hex code and create **tints and shades** (lighter and darker versions) for backgrounds, borders and hover states. Save them as colour styles in your design tool.

### Colour meaning is contextual

Colour associations vary across cultures, industries and personal experience. Green may suggest nature, money or health; white is associated with purity in some contexts and mourning in others; red can mean danger, celebration, love or a sale. Rather than relying on generic "colour psychology" lists, consider your audience, your category conventions and your competitors. Sometimes breaking a category's colour convention helps you stand out; sometimes it confuses buyers.

### Worked example: a palette for a halal food blog

Audience: families in the UK and the Gulf; tone: warm, appetising, trustworthy.

- Primary: a warm terracotta (appetising, earthy).
- Accent: saffron yellow for highlights and "Get the recipe" buttons.
- Neutrals: charcoal for text, warm grey for secondary text, cream for backgrounds.
- Distribution: cream backgrounds (60%), food photography and terracotta panels (30%), saffron accents (10%).
- Greyscale check: charcoal on cream passes easily; saffron text on cream fails — so saffron is used for button backgrounds with charcoal text instead.

### Tints, shades and tones in practice

A **tint** adds white to a colour, a **shade** adds black, and a **tone** adds grey. Building a short ramp of each brand colour — for example five steps from very light to very dark — gives you backgrounds, borders, hover states and text colours that all feel related. Name the steps consistently (for example "coral-100" to "coral-900") so everyone on a team picks the same values. Light tints make calm section backgrounds; dark shades often become your accessible text colours. This one habit removes most of the guesswork when a design needs "a slightly lighter version" of a brand colour.

### Common mistakes

- Choosing colours by hue alone and ignoring value contrast.
- Using saturated colours everywhere, which is tiring to look at.
- Pure black (#000000) on pure white for large areas can feel harsh; near-black and off-white are often more comfortable while still high contrast.
- Relying on generic colour-psychology claims instead of audience context.

### Summary

Think in hue, saturation and value; start from a harmony; use a 60-30-10 distribution; build a small palette with tints and shades; and always check value contrast.
keyTakeaways: Every colour has hue, saturation and value — value drives legibility.
Export for screens in sRGB; CMYK is for print.
Use harmonies (analogous, complementary, etc.) as starting points and 60-30-10 for distribution.
Colour meaning depends on culture, category and audience — avoid generic psychology claims.

knowledgeCheck.question: Two colours look very different but text in one on the other is hard to read. What is the most likely reason?
options: They have similar value (lightness)
They are in the CMYK model
They are too saturated to display
They are complementary hues
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Legibility depends mainly on lightness difference. Different hues with similar value produce weak contrast; a greyscale check reveals this.

knowledgeCheck.question: In the 60-30-10 guideline, what is the 10% typically used for?
options: Photography
Body text
Background
Accent elements such as calls to action and highlights
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The small 10% share is for accents that should stand out. The 60% is usually background/neutral and 30% supporting colour.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which colour space should you usually export social media graphics in?
options: Greyscale
Pantone
CMYK
sRGB
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Screens and most platforms expect sRGB. CMYK is for print; Pantone is a spot-colour system; greyscale removes colour.

lessons.activity: Create a palette for your brand with one primary, one accent and four neutrals. Build a sample post using 60-30-10, then convert it to greyscale to check value contrast.

lessons.title: Accessible contrast and inclusive colour use
lessons.body:
### Why accessibility is a design requirement

A significant share of people have some form of visual impairment, colour vision deficiency, or situational limits such as bright sunlight, a cracked screen or a low-brightness setting. Designs with weak contrast exclude these viewers and perform worse for everyone. Accessibility is also increasingly a legal expectation for websites and apps in many jurisdictions, and a reputational one everywhere.

### WCAG contrast ratios

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), published by the W3C, are the widely used international standard. WCAG 2.2 is the current recommendation. For contrast, the key success criteria at level AA are:

| Content | Minimum ratio (AA) | Enhanced (AAA) |
|---|---|---|
| Normal text | 4.5 : 1 | 7 : 1 |
| Large text (about 24 px regular, or about 18.66 px bold and above) | 3 : 1 | 4.5 : 1 |
| User-interface components and meaningful graphics (icons, input borders, chart lines) | 3 : 1 | — |

Contrast ratio ranges from 1:1 (no contrast — same colour) to 21:1 (black on white). These criteria were written for web content, but they are an excellent benchmark for social graphics, slides and ads too.

Note that WCAG 3 is in development and explores a different contrast model; until it becomes a recommendation, WCAG 2.x ratios remain the reference.

### How to check contrast

1. Pick the text colour and the background colour (for text on photos, sample the lightest and darkest areas behind the text).
2. Enter both into a contrast checker — many free web tools, browser developer tools, and design-tool plugins exist.
3. Compare against the table above.
4. Adjust **value** (lighter or darker), not just hue, until it passes.

```
Contrast check log
Element:        ______________
Text colour:    #______   Background: #______
Size/weight:    ______ (normal or large?)
Ratio:          ____ : 1
Pass AA?        [ ] yes  [ ] no → adjustment: __________
```

### Colour vision deficiency

Colour vision deficiencies (often called colour blindness) affect a meaningful minority of people, more commonly men. Red–green deficiencies are the most common. Design implications:

- **Never use colour as the only way to convey meaning.** A chart where "profit" is green and "loss" is red needs labels, patterns or icons too. A form error needs text, not just a red border.
- Test with a colour-blindness simulator (available in many design tools, browser developer tools and plugins).
- Prefer palettes that differ in lightness as well as hue.

### Common accessible-colour patterns

- Dark text on light backgrounds for body copy.
- If using white text, place it on sufficiently dark backgrounds — many mid-tone brand colours (bright orange, light green, sky blue) fail with white text at normal sizes.
- Reserve bright, light accent colours for large shapes or button backgrounds with dark text.
- Create an accessible variant of your brand colour (slightly darker or lighter) for text use if the main colour fails.

### Worked example: an orange brand button

A brand's orange (a mid-lightness orange) with white "Book now" text at 16 px fails 4.5:1.

Options:

1. Darken the orange for the button until white text passes — keeps white text, slightly changes the brand shade (define it as "orange-700" in the palette).
2. Keep the orange and use near-black text — often passes easily and keeps the brand colour.
3. Make the text large and bold enough to count as large text and check against 3:1 — acceptable for short labels but not for body copy.

Document the decision in the brand's colour guidance so everyone uses the accessible pairing.

### Beyond contrast

- Avoid flashing content: WCAG includes limits on flashing (no more than three flashes per second, with thresholds) because it can trigger seizures.
- Don't put important text over animated backgrounds.
- Provide captions for video and alt text for images.

### Common mistakes

- Checking contrast against the average colour of a photo instead of its lightest/darkest area behind the text.
- Assuming a brand colour "must" be used for text even when it fails.
- Using red/green alone for status.
- Treating accessibility as optional polish at the end of a project.

### Summary

Use WCAG 2.2 AA ratios — 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and meaningful graphics — as your baseline, never rely on colour alone, simulate colour-vision deficiencies, and create accessible variants of brand colours where needed.
keyTakeaways: WCAG 2.2 AA: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and meaningful UI/graphics.
Fix contrast by adjusting lightness (value), not just hue.
Never use colour as the only means of conveying meaning.
Create accessible variants of brand colours and document approved pairings.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the WCAG 2.2 AA minimum contrast ratio for normal-sized body text?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text; 3:1 applies to large text and UI/graphics; 7:1 is AAA for normal text; 21:1 is the maximum possible.

knowledgeCheck.question: A dashboard shows good results in green and bad results in red with no other cue. What is the accessibility problem?
options: Charts cannot use colour
The colours are not on-brand
Colour is the only way meaning is conveyed, which excludes people with colour vision deficiency
The contrast ratio is automatically too high
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Meaning must not rely on colour alone; add labels, icons or patterns. Colour can still be used, and brand fit is a separate question.

knowledgeCheck.question: White text on a brand's light green button fails contrast. Which fix keeps the result accessible and on-brand?
options: Make the text thinner
Use near-black text on the green, or define a darker green variant for white text
Reduce the button size
Add a glow around the text
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Changing lightness — dark text or a darker variant — fixes contrast while retaining the brand hue. Thinner text, glows and smaller buttons make things worse.

lessons.activity: Run your brand colours through a contrast checker in every text/background combination you use. Record results in the contrast log and define an accessible variant for any failing pairing.

lessons.title: Colour in practice: hierarchy, mood and consistency
lessons.body:
### From palette to real designs

Knowing theory is one thing; using colour well across dozens of posts is another. This lesson turns your palette into repeatable decisions.

### Colour creates hierarchy

Colour is a hierarchy lever alongside size and weight:

- **Accent = action or key info.** If the accent appears everywhere, it stops meaning anything.
- **Neutrals carry content.** Most text should be near-black or near-white depending on background.
- **Muted versus saturated:** saturated colours advance; muted colours recede. Use muted backgrounds so content pops.
- **Warm versus cool:** warm colours (reds, oranges, yellows) tend to feel closer and more energetic; cool colours (blues, greens) tend to recede and feel calmer.

### Colour and mood — by context

Instead of relying on universal "meanings", build mood with combinations:

| Desired mood | Typical approach |
|---|---|
| Calm, trustworthy | Cool hues, moderate saturation, plenty of light neutrals |
| Energetic, urgent | Warm, saturated accents, high value contrast |
| Premium, minimal | Restrained palette, dark or off-white backgrounds, one refined accent |
| Playful, youthful | Brighter triadic combinations, rounded shapes |
| Natural, organic | Earthy analogous hues, muted saturation, textures |

Always test with your actual audience and category; conventions vary by market.

### Colour in photography and imagery

Imagery often contributes the 30% in 60-30-10. Harmonise it with your palette:

- Choose photos whose dominant colours sit comfortably with your brand palette.
- Apply a consistent **photo treatment** — the same warmth, contrast and saturation adjustments, or a consistent preset — across a series.
- Use **duotones** or colour overlays for graphic consistency when mixing photos from different sources (keep overlays subtle so faces look natural).
- Watch skin tones: heavy colour grading can make skin look unnatural; always check people look like themselves.

### Consistency across a series

For recognisability, lock a small set of rules:

```
Series colour rules (example)
Backgrounds:   off-white or deep navy only
Headline:      navy on off-white / off-white on navy
Accent:        coral — max 1–2 uses per slide (key word, CTA)
Charts:        navy, coral, grey (with labels)
Photos:        warm preset "A", saturation −10
Never:         coral text on off-white (fails contrast)
```

### Dark mode and platform backgrounds

Your design will be seen on light and dark app themes. Test how your post looks against both: a pure white design can look like a glaring block in dark mode; a design with transparent edges (such as PNG stickers) can change appearance. Designing with your own solid background and some internal margin keeps things predictable.

### Colour for data and charts

When you share charts or infographics:

- Use one highlight colour for the data point that matters, with other data in greys.
- Order colours logically (light to dark for low to high values).
- Label directly on the chart where possible instead of relying on a legend matched by colour.
- Check accessibility with a colour-blindness simulator.

### Worked example: making a stat pop

A carousel slide says "Our clients cut editing time by around half" with a bar chart of before/after. (Illustrative figures should be labelled as such, and any real claim must be supported by evidence.)

- Background: deep navy (60%).
- Bars: "before" in muted grey, "after" in coral (the one thing to notice).
- Labels: off-white text directly on bars.
- Headline: off-white, with the key phrase "around half" in coral.
- Everything else neutral, so the eye goes straight to the coral elements.

### A five-minute colour review

Before publishing any design, run this quick review. First, view it in greyscale to confirm the value structure still shows the hierarchy. Second, count how many times the accent colour appears — if it is more than two or three, remove some. Third, compare the post with the previous three in your feed to check the photo treatment and palette match. Fourth, check any text-on-colour pairing against your approved contrast list. This review takes minutes and catches most colour problems before your audience sees them.

### Common mistakes

- Accent colour used on every element.
- Inconsistent photo editing within a series.
